title: Irrigation Water Withdrawals for Fruits, Vegetables, and Tree Nuts in the Continental United States From 2008 to 2020
content:
Abstract

Irrigation represents a major use of water in the United States, yet irrigation water withdrawals are poorly characterized for individual crops. This study estimates irrigation water withdrawals for fruits, vegetables, and tree nut crops grown in the United States. We quantify surface water withdrawals, groundwater withdrawals, and nonrenewable groundwater depletion (GWD) for 65 crops at the county scale across the continental United States from 2008 to 2020. Estimates are generated using a physical irrigation model that disaggregates aggregate irrigation withdrawals for crop categories into individual crops based on crop-specific irrigated area and relative evapotranspiration rates derived from crop coefficients. Over the study period, irrigation water use for specialty crops was highly concentrated, with only a handful of crops accounting for the majority of withdrawals within most counties. Almonds, grapes, and walnuts account for nearly 50% of all GWD across specialty crops. 49 out of 65 produce crops (75%) rely on groundwater where at least half of the withdrawals are depletionary, raising sustainability concerns. Crop-level disaggregation also revealed structural differences between perennial and annual crops. This study presents the first national-scale, crop-specific assessment of irrigation water withdrawals for fruits, vegetables, and tree nuts by water source, county, and year. Because crop-specific ground-truth irrigation data are unavailable, estimates should be interpreted as relative, best-available estimates rather than direct measurements; sources of uncertainty are discussed and, where possible, quantified. The resulting data set provides a foundation for future research and for informing assessments of agricultural water use and groundwater sustainability.
